content.thinking:
Okay, the fetcher script has finished. I need to verify that it actually retrieved all the required assets before moving on. The background task output shows a series of lines like “sprite 150/151”, “sprite 146/151”, etc., ending with “sprite 151/151” and then “Done. Wrote pokedex.js (151 mons), moves.js (273 moves).” That indicates the script iterated through all 151 Pokémon and wrote the data files.

Next, I used PowerShell to query the counts of the sprite directories and the file sizes of the generated data files. The results are:
- Front sprites count: 151
- Back sprites count: 151
- pokedex.js length: 83696 bytes
- moves.js length: 87899 bytes

These numbers confirm that every front and back sprite is present and that the pokédex and moves data files were successfully written. Since the user wants a full Pokémon FireRed remake with all 151 Gen‑1 monsters, I now have the core asset foundation ready: sprites, Pokémon stats, and move definitions.

The next logical step is to start building the game engine. The engine has many components (overworld map, player movement, battle system, UI, etc.), but it makes sense to begin with the most fundamental data structure that will be used throughout: the type effectiveness chart. The battle system will need to know how each type interacts with every other type (e.g., Fire is super effective against Grass, not very effective against Water, etc.). By defining this chart first, I can later plug it into the damage calculation logic when I get to battles.

Therefore, I should inform the user that all assets have been successfully fetched and then state that I’m moving on to the engine, starting with the type chart. This directly follows from the verification I just performed and sets a clear next milestone.

content.text: All assets landed: 151 front sprites, 151 back sprites, full pokédex and 273 moves. Now the engine — type chart first:
